claim: Reasoning-model traces map onto Schoenfeld episodes (Read, Analyze, Plan, Implement, Explore, Verify, Monitor) with sticky, ordered sentence transitions (Implement stays Implement 0.63, Plan goes to Implement 0.40, Explore goes to Analyze 0.25). Basis is 38 hand-labelled R1 responses.
agent_test: Log our agent's own state sequence in the same 7 labels on 50 SAT-style items and check the transition matrix looks like the human-labelled one.

claim: Sentence-level episode labelling by an LLM is feasible but not perfect: GPT-4.1 with examples and guidebook gets 0.805 accuracy and kappa 0.764 on a 30% test split of 38 responses (about 11 responses), while the same setup scores 0.681 in the all-data table; on a larger gold set of 7,067 sentences GPT-5 and GPT-4.1 reach about 86%. Same research group for both. Update: Table 2 (0.681) is all annotated data and Table 4 (0.805) is the 30% test subset, so they are different evaluation sets; on the larger ThinkARM gold set (7,067 sentences, eight labels) GPT-4.1 gets 86.10% / kappa 82.74. Fine-tuned BERT reaches 0.732 / kappa 0.671, below our 0.75 gating bar.
agent_test: Label 200 of our traces with a cheap labeller and a strong one; require kappa above 0.75 between them before using labels to gate anything.

claim: Verify is the hardest label boundary: Analyze-to-Verify (4.8% of all sentences) and Implement-to-Verify (3.2%) are the largest confusions. A detector that depends on Verify labels inherits this noise.
agent_test: Double-label Verify to measure noise; count Verify only when a check is explicit (plug-back, recompute, different method).

claim: A written guidebook raises LLM labelling accuracy more than in-context examples (GPT-4.1 sentence accuracy 0.595 base, 0.604 with examples, 0.676 with guidebook, 0.681 with both).
agent_test: Write the monitor prompt as explicit definitions with contrast rules (Explore vs Verify) rather than few-shot examples; compare the two at equal tokens.

claim: Reasoning models spread tokens over Analyze, Explore and Verify, while instruction models are Implement-heavy and almost never Explore or Verify. On easy GSM8K items Qwen3-32B in reasoning mode spends 55.89% of tokens on Verify.
agent_test: Record episode shares for our agent on easy and hard items; cap Verify share on easy items and see if accuracy holds at fewer tokens.

claim: Wrong answers are longer and switch thoughts more than right ones (225% more tokens, 418% more thought switches for o1-like models), and within a fixed question longer chains and more review go with lower accuracy. The within-question control (Feng) and same-question length study (Hassid) agree with the raw correlation (Wang), so length is not only a difficulty effect.
agent_test: Log tokens and switches per item; on matched items check that wrong runs show more switches; use a switch-rate threshold as one input to a stop-or-replan rule.

claim: Models often hold a correct thought and then abandon it: over 70% of wrong responses contain at least one correct thought, and models keep generating after a correct solution is injected into the chain. Qualitative agreement; the 70% figure comes from one paper and few models.
agent_test: Test an operator that freezes an independently checked intermediate answer as a candidate and requires a stated reason before dropping it.

claim: The share of steps in abandoned branches (Failed-Step Fraction) predicts correctness better than length or review ratio, and deleting failed branches from wrong traces raises continuation accuracy (R1 20.89% to 29.42%). A second group's tree features also predict correctness and name four error shapes (over-branching, step redundancy, direct reasoning, skipped thinking). Update: the same paper has a summary arm; replacing the failed branch with a short summary keeps 85% (first) and 92% (last) of the delete gain for R1 (28.14 and 22.57 vs 29.42 and 23.75), but only 17% and 81% for GPT-oss-120B.
agent_test: After an abandoned branch, replace its text in context with a one-line dead-end note; compare with keeping the full text at equal tokens.

claim: Overthinking on easy problems: the first solution round is already correct in over 92% of cases and uses under 60% of tokens; later rounds add little. Several independent papers report extra compute with no gain on simple items.
agent_test: Add a difficulty-aware stop: after the first checked answer on an easy item, stop; compare accuracy and tokens with always-continue.

claim: Reflection after a first answer is mostly confirmatory: over 90% of reflections keep the answer and corrective ones (wrong to right) are mostly under 2%, using 16.8-47.8% of tokens for 1.4-3.5% accuracy. Independent overthinking work finds first-correct plus reflection beats first-correct alone by only 1.4% on the hard MATH500 set.
agent_test: Count how often our verify step changes the answer. If under 5% of cases, make verification conditional on a risk signal.

claim: Forcing extra thinking ('Wait') first helps then hurts in one study (GSM8K 82.2% at 385 tokens, 87.3% at about 1,100, 70.3% at about 15,980), while budget forcing in s1 raised AIME24 from 50% to 57%. Sources differ on the sign beyond the first extension; the likely moderator is starting budget and model.
agent_test: Run budget extension at 1x, 2x, 4x on our agent and plot accuracy by difficulty to find where extra turns stop paying.

claim: Episode ratios and transitions predict correctness in a Lasso on 500 traces from 5 models: Explore-to-Monitor +0.41, Explore-to-Analyze +0.31, Explore ratio -0.54, Explore-to-Verify -0.45. No held-out accuracy or AUC is reported, and the positive Verify ratio (+0.21) sits against the negative review-ratio finding of Feng et al. Update: two held-out cousins exist. Bloom-step features reach AUC 0.676 vs 0.613 for length alone (nested CV, 9,132 samples, math); ReasonOps operator features reach within-problem AUC 0.701 vs 0.551 for length. Both gains are modest, neither uses Schoenfeld labels, and no held-out test of Schoenfeld-label features exists.
agent_test: Fit our own model on our logs with a held-out split and report AUC; keep only features that beat a length-only baseline.

claim: Efficiency methods remove different episodes. L1 (2,437 tokens) and ThinkPrune (4,054) cut Analyze and Verify from baseline (Verify 11.43% to 6.99% and 8.37%); Arora and Zanette (5,312) stays closer to baseline (Verify 9.94%). CORRECTED: the earlier statement that Monitor rises from 1.84% to 8.52% under L1 was a column misread. 8.52% is the Answer share (baseline 3.80%); Monitor stays at 1.64% (L1), 1.80% (ThinkPrune), 1.64% (Arora-Zanette) against 1.84% baseline.
agent_test: Compare our reduced-budget runs by episode profile as well as accuracy, to see what is cut.

claim: Sentence-level counterfactual resampling shows plan-generation and uncertainty-management (backtracking) sentences carry more causal weight than computation sentences. One 14B model, 20 MATH problems.
agent_test: Resample after our plan and replan steps to see whether they change the final answer more than ordinary steps.

claim: Four behaviours (verification, backtracking, subgoal setting, backward chaining) predict whether a base model improves under RL, and priming with wrong but well-structured solutions works about as well as correct ones. A 28-element taxonomy over 192,709 traces finds models under-use elements that correlate with success.
agent_test: Ablate each of our operators on a fixed item set and see which removal hurts at equal tokens.

claim: Wandering has a formal account: a depth-first explorer with a wandering parameter reaches a success plateau then fails as problem depth grows; failures are invalid exploration, not just length.
agent_test: Add a revisit counter (same state or sub-goal tried again) and test whether it separates failed from solved runs.

claim: Models underthink hard problems and overthink easy ones, so length is poorly calibrated to difficulty. Missing-premise questions produce answers 2 to 4 times longer, and GPT-o1 abstains far more than R1 and QwQ.
agent_test: Include unsolvable items and test whether our agent flags the missing premise before burning budget.

claim: A small probe on hidden states predicts whether an intermediate answer is correct (AUC above 0.7, above 0.9 for one model on AIME), and confidence-based early exit (DEER) cuts tokens 24-39% at equal or better accuracy. Two independent groups. Both need model internals or an answer-probing call.
agent_test: Probe the agent with a trial-answer call at each phase and stop when the answer is stable twice; compare tokens at equal accuracy.

claim: Thought-switch penalties at decoding (TIP) give modest gains (AIME2024 QwQ 38.3 to 44.1, R1 73.8 to 74.8). Decoding is outside a scaffold, so only the idea transfers. Update: on R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B (AIME24) a bare prompt rule ('explore each idea thoroughly before moving on') gave 29.0 vs vanilla 28.9, TIP 31.3, and a PRM-scored switch intervention 40.0; intervening at every switch lowered AIME25 accuracy (20.0 to 18.9).
agent_test: Prompt-level rule: finish or explicitly abandon a thought before starting another; check that switches fall.

claim: In agent loops overthinking takes three forms (Analysis Paralysis, Rogue Actions, Premature Disengagement), and picking the lower-overthinking trajectory gains almost 30% on SWE-Bench Verified. Seen only on a project page.
agent_test: Add the three labels to our impasse record and see which dominate in our failures.

claim: Repetition loops are detectable with cheap signals (n-gram repetition, loop-stop at K=2 repeated sub-thoughts). Measured detectors exist only as white-box probes: a linear probe on the paragraph-break hidden state flags word-salad chunks at 92.72/92.31/89.77/93.52% accuracy (GSM8K/MATH-500/AIME25/GPQA, Qwen-7B distill, temp 0), falling to 77.96% on AIME25 at temp 0.6 and about 83% on Qwen3-8B; ROM's boundary probe reaches AUROC 0.928. Labels are machine-made, not human stuck points, and no precision or recall is reported for any text-only detector.
agent_test: Build the n-gram plus revisit-count detector, hand-label 100 traces, and report precision and recall before wiring it to an action.

claim: No validated coded impasse or wild-goose-chase detector built from Schoenfeld labels exists in the sources found. The evidence supports a composite of cheap signals: thought-switch rate, Explore share, failed-branch share, repeated n-grams, answer-confirmed-then-continue. Update: no precision or recall was found for the composite either. Closest measured signals: wait and backtrack counts (within-problem AUC 0.603 and 0.594 vs length 0.551), Evaluate/Analyze oscillation (negative coefficients), and half-trace operator features (WP-AUC 0.664).
agent_test: Compose these five signals, run on held-out traces from our agent, and compare against a length-only rule at equal tokens.

claim: Schoenfeld's human finding that control (planning, monitoring, evaluating) rather than knowledge separates experts from novices, and that many student attempts never monitor a chosen path, is known here only second-hand; the original book and chapters were not opened.
agent_test: No direct test; treat as motivation only.

claim: Step-type features beat length alone for predicting correctness only by a modest margin, and only in studies with held-out folds. Bloom-level shares plus transitions: AUC 0.676 vs 0.613 length-only (accuracy 0.631 vs 0.623, F1 0.667 vs 0.666). ReasonOps operators: within-problem AUC 0.701 vs 0.551 for length; counts of wait (0.603) and backtrack (0.594) beat length. A model judging its own trace is at chance (0.512). Nothing is held-out for Schoenfeld labels specifically.
agent_test: Log Schoenfeld-style labels for 200 runs of our agent, fit a logistic model with problem-grouped folds, and report within-problem AUC against length and wait-count baselines.

claim: Reflection value depends on item difficulty. On easy problems correct traces are forward-stepping (committal-minus-reflective gap +44.2% vs +7.5%, AUC 0.76); on hard problems the gap carries no signal (AUC 0.48) and only hypothesizing seems to help. Half a trace carries most of the correctness signal (WP-AUC 0.664 at 50% vs 0.701 at 100%).
agent_test: Make the review-loop cap depend on a difficulty estimate (pass rate over N cheap samples) and compare with a fixed cap at equal tokens.

claim: Review in Feng et al. (reads, checks, restates, deletes or rewinds without advancing) is broader than Schoenfeld Verify (checking phrases), so 'review hurts' and 'Verify helps' are not directly in conflict. The Answer episode separates a check after an answer (final check) from earlier checks, but no study has varied check position under control.
agent_test: Three arms at equal tokens: no check, one final check, up to K mid-trace checks. Compare accuracy and tokens.

claim: Agentic overthinking has a coded judge (Analysis Paralysis, Rogue Actions, Premature Disengagement, score 0-10) validated on 20 traces by four experts with only a correlation plot reported. Ranking runs by lowest score gives 27.3% (k=2 low effort, 43% cheaper) and 30.3% (k=3) on SWE-bench Verified. Whether Schoenfeld episode statistics transfer to code or agent tasks is untested; ReasonOps shows predictive signal on LiveCodeBench (WP-AUC 0.795 within-dataset) but near chance on BBH and HumanEval.
agent_test: Run the same episode labeller on 50 coding and 50 planning runs of our agent and compare transition matrices with the math one.

claim: Schoenfeld human baseline numbers could not be verified: the author's Berkeley PDFs returned 404, Harskamp and Suhre returned 403, and search quota and APIs were rate-limited. The claim that many novice attempts show no monitoring stays unquantified.
agent_test: Read the 1985 book chapter or the 1992 chapter directly and extract the timeline-graph counts before quoting any percentage.

claim: Probe-based stopping needs weights. Hidden-state detectors work (ROM probe 85.9% / AUROC 0.928; word-salad probe 78-93%), but a black-box scaffold only sees text. Whether a text-only stop probe matches them is untested here.
agent_test: Compare a DEER-style answer-stability stop against n-gram repetition and fixed-budget stops on 100 items at equal tokens.
